context_title: canonical large language model neural network architecture families

entries.query: canonical large language model neural network architecture families
entries.answer:
Large language models (LLMs) descend from a small number of canonical neural network architecture families, each defined by how attention flows through the network, what training objective is used, and what kinds of tasks the resulting model handles best. The modern landscape is dominated by the **decoder-only transformer**, but understanding all major families is essential to grasp why the field evolved the way it did.
## The Original Transformer
The foundational architecture, introduced in *Attention Is All You Need* (2017), pairs a full **encoder** with a full **decoder**. The encoder reads the entire input sequence with bidirectional (unrestricted) self-attention, producing a rich contextual embedding of it. The decoder then generates an output sequence token by token, attending both to its own previously generated tokens (via *masked* self-attention) and to the encoder's output (via cross-attention). This design was conceived for sequence-to-sequence tasks like machine translation, and it is the structural parent of every architecture family that followed.[1]
## Encoder-Only Models
Encoder-only architectures strip away the decoder entirely and retain only the bidirectional self-attention stack. Because every token can attend to every other token in the input, these models build deeply contextualized representations, making them ideal for *understanding* tasks: classification, named entity recognition, and extractive question answering.[2]

The canonical example is **BERT** (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), pretrained with masked language modeling — randomly masking ~15% of tokens and training the model to predict them from surrounding context — and a next-sentence prediction objective. **RoBERTa** removed the next-sentence task and scaled the training data, improving downstream performance without changing the architecture. Modern descendants like **ModernBERT** continue this line. The key limitation is that these models do not perform autoregressive generation; they are not "LLMs" in the generative chat-assistant sense, even though they are transformer language models.[1][2]
## Decoder-Only Models
Decoder-only architectures are the dominant paradigm for modern generative LLMs. They use *causal* (left-to-right, masked) self-attention: each token can only attend to tokens that precede it in the sequence. This autoregressive property means the model is trained simply to predict the next token, yet that objective alone produces emergent capabilities — summarization, translation, reasoning, code generation — at sufficient scale.[3][1]

The **GPT family** (GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-4) pioneered this approach. Modern refinements consolidate around a set of upgrades over the original GPT design: **RoPE** (Rotary Position Embeddings) replaces learned absolute positional encodings for better length generalization; **RMSNorm** replaces LayerNorm for training stability; **SwiGLU/SiLU** activations replace ReLU in the feed-forward blocks; and **Grouped Query Attention (GQA)** reduces the KV-cache memory footprint during inference. Models like **LLaMA**, **Gemma**, **Qwen**, and **DeepSeek V3** all share this refined decoder-only blueprint.[4][2][5][1]
## Encoder-Decoder (Seq2Seq) Models
Encoder-decoder hybrids preserve the full original architecture but are trained with modern objectives. **T5** (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer) reframes *every* NLP task as a "text-to-text" problem — the encoder reads a prefixed input like `"summarize: <article>"` and the decoder generates the output text — allowing a single model to handle translation, classification, summarization, and QA. **BART** uses a denoising objective: the encoder receives corrupted text and the decoder reconstructs the original, making it especially strong for generation tasks like summarization.[6][2][7]

These models excel when the output depends heavily on a complex, potentially long input — the encoder compresses that input into a rich representation that the decoder can consult at every generation step via cross-attention. Recent work at Google showed that adapting decoder-only LLMs (like Gemma 2) into encoder-decoder form after pretraining yields substantial quality gains, especially after instruction tuning, because the architecture better balances quality and inference efficiency.[5]
## State Space Models (SSMs)
A more recent family departs from attention altogether. **State Space Models**, epitomized by **Mamba** (2023), replace the \( O(n^2) \) attention mechanism with a recurrent formulation based on linear dynamical systems. The core idea is a *selective* state-space layer: the model learns input-dependent transition matrices, so it can decide what information to retain in a fixed-size hidden state as it processes a sequence. This gives Mamba **linear-time** inference and constant memory in the sequence length — a major efficiency advantage over standard attention for very long contexts. SSMs are best understood as a learned continuous-time recurrence, somewhat analogous to LSTMs but far more expressive and parallelizable during training.[8][9]
## Mixture of Experts (MoE)
MoE is not a separate architecture family so much as a **sparsity technique** that overlays any of the above. In a standard transformer, every token passes through every feed-forward layer. In an MoE model, each feed-forward block is replaced by a collection of \(N\) "expert" sub-networks, and a learned **router** selects only \(k \ll N\) of them per token. This lets a model have a very large *total* parameter count while only activating a small fraction per forward pass. **DeepSeek V3**, for instance, uses 671B total parameters but only ~37B active per token. MoE can also be applied to SSMs: **BlackMamba** combines a Mamba SSM backbone with MoE feed-forward layers, inheriting the reduced training and inference FLOPs of both techniques simultaneously.[4][8][10]
## Hybrid and Emerging Architectures
The frontier of LLM architecture research blurs the lines between families. **Hybrid Conv+Attention** models (like LFM2) interleave convolutional and attention layers, offering local feature extraction plus global context. **Diffusion LMs** like dLLM treat generation as a masked-diffusion process rather than autoregressive next-token prediction, enabling parallel token generation. Research into **Canon layers** — depthwise causal convolutions inserted into a transformer — shows consistent improvements in factuality without major accuracy trade-offs.[4]
## Architecture Family at a Glance
| Family | Attention Direction | Training Objective | Primary Strength | Representative Models |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Encoder-only | Bidirectional | Masked LM | Text understanding, embeddings | BERT, RoBERTa, ModernBERT |
| Decoder-only | Causal (left-to-right) | Next token prediction | Text generation, reasoning | GPT-4, LLaMA, Gemma, Qwen |
| Encoder-Decoder | Encoder: bi; Decoder: causal + cross | Denoising / text-to-text | Translation, summarization | T5, BART, mBART |
| State Space (SSM) | None (recurrent state) | Next token prediction | Long-context, efficient inference | Mamba, RWKV |
| Mixture of Experts | Depends on backbone | Depends on backbone | Scale with sparse compute | DeepSeek V3, Mixtral, BlackMamba |

Importantly, at small scales (~70M parameters), all architecture families perform within ~2% of each other on standard benchmarks. The architectural choices that distinguish LLaMA3 from GPT-2 (RoPE, RMSNorm, GQA) are engineered to matter at 7B+ parameters, where inference efficiency, long-context handling, and training stability all become pressing concerns.[4]
